PullRequest.Title: chat: keep working progress above the composer
PullRequest.Body:

## Motivation

Related to #342958 as part of the motion housekeeping work.

The existing animated logo and progress message provide useful status, but disappear when the conversation scrolls away from the latest turn. Keep that component visible above the composer and reference chips while reading earlier messages, rather than adding another indicator.

Once #342958 turns off the glowing composer border, the sticky logo and progress message will still provide clearly visible status regardless of conversation scroll position. Further motion simplifications remain separate work.

## Changes

- Relocate the existing working-progress component above the references and composer in bottom-composer Chat layouts, in both main-window Chat and the Agents window.
- Keep the existing progress wording, animation, reduced-motion handling, background activity, and approval states.
- Clear the sticky status on completion, cancellation, or session replacement. Resume it after answering questions or reviewing plans without waiting for another provider update.
- Preserve transcript progress in read-only chats and existing behavior when persistent progress is Off or the layout is minimal or input-on-top.
- Update accessibility help and add lifecycle, state-transition, virtualization, and host-alignment regression coverage.

## Testing

1. Set `chat.experimental.persistentProgress` to `draw`. In main-window Chat, attach a file reference and start a request that produces a long response. Repeat in the Agents window with reference chips above the composer.
2. Scroll up to earlier messages while the request is running. The working logo and latest status should remain above the reference chips, aligned with the composer. Check that the same provider status is not repeated in the transcript.
3. Narrow the window with a long status message. Check wrapping, spacing above the chips, and alignment in Light 2026, Dark 2026, and Default High Contrast.
4. Complete or stop the request, then switch sessions during another request. The status should clear without leaving stale content or an empty status row.
5. Set persistent progress to `off` and confirm no sticky working row appears. Enable reduced motion and confirm the status remains visible without animation. Check that read-only chats retain transcript progress.
6. Answer a question or approve a plan during a request. The status should resume before new provider output arrives.

Native Code OSS validation exercised both Chat hosts, scrolling with reference chips and a file attachment, long-status wrapping in narrow layouts, theme changes, and completion cleanup. Targeted regression tests cover status ownership, reused progress parts, accessibility announcements, configuration transitions, and completion.

## Visual evidence

The clips compare the original pre-change behavior with this PR. Both use native Code OSS and a local test conversation with earlier turns, provider progress, background activity, reference chips, and a file attachment. Before captures restore the original behavioral modules and styles in the same native build; they are not a CSS-only simulation.

### Main-window Chat — Light 2026, scrolling

**Before — original behavior:** the working status belongs to the response and scrolls away.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e7ad09b0-df9c-4b12-92f5-8f5321a0ba5c

**After:** one existing working status stays above the reference chips and composer as earlier messages scroll.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f2f6690f-d92a-4968-836b-0e3f4cd24259

### Agents window — Light 2026, scrolling

**Before — original behavior:** scrolling to earlier messages removes the current working status from view.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/785a4014-0221-4029-9b6d-0bebbae08dd4

**After:** the working status remains above the production reference-chip row, sharing the composer's leading edge.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0e456bab-a677-42ec-b130-2d5d2706138e

### Narrow layouts — after

**Agents window, Dark 2026:** a long status wraps above the reference chips without a second transcript status.

![Agents window, Dark 2026: status wrapping above reference chips](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ea8bf608-96f8-4c60-ae52-868dd3cd7e83)

![Main-window Chat, Default High Contrast: status wrapping above reference chips](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4589d4c4-2702-4bdd-8c53-28b591a633d6)

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The event path is direct: each non-quiet response content update fires ChatResponseModel.onDidChange, ChatResponseViewModel forwards it to ChatViewModel.onDidChange, and the added signal synchronously reruns this autorun. ChatViewModel invalidates its getItems cache before listeners run, while updateStickyProgress annotates and repeatedly scans the full response. The exact millisecond cost varies with provider chunking and response size, but the multiplicative work and main-thread reachability are established.
Findings.PerformanceResource: main-thread CPU plus temporary arrays, annotated content objects, and MarkdownString allocations
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For E streamed response mutations, T visible transcript items, and P accumulated response parts, the added path performs O(E*(T+P)) work: getItems rebuilds its invalidated visible-items cache, the autorun scans P tool states, annotateSpecialMarkdownContent recreates the P-part annotated array, and getPersistentWorkingProgress performs several more P-sized scans. Provider token/progress updates make E large, while agent sessions with many tool calls make P realistically large.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased main-thread CPU and GC pressure during response streaming, causing delayed token rendering and potential dropped frames in long agent conversations
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Persistent progress lived in the rendered response and was updated as part of the list's existing render pass; when that response was virtualized away there was no independent renderer-level listener reprocessing the entire response on every model mutation.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The added Event.any(viewModel.onDidChange, configuration changes) signal drives an unthrottled autorun for every chat model change. Each run locates the latest response, subscribes by scanning all of its tool/elicitation parts, then updateStickyProgress locates it again, annotates the complete response, derives progress through multiple full-array scans, and only afterward lets updateWorkingContent discover that the displayed label may be unchanged.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 1238 adds a signal over the broad viewModel.onDidChange event; the added autorun at lines 1239-1249 calls updateStickyProgress for every signal, and added lines 1259-1260 rebuild annotated content and derive progress from the full response before any unchanged-content short circuit.
Findings.Title: Coalesce sticky-progress updates during streaming
Findings.Impact: During a long tool-heavy agent response, each streamed token/progress chunk repeats collection-wide work even if the sticky text remains “Working.” Users can see slower streaming updates and UI jank as accumulated response parts and transcript length grow.
Findings.Evidence: ChatModel.acceptResponseProgress calls Response.updateContent; Response._contentChanged fires onDidChangeValue for each non-quiet chunk; ChatResponseModel forwards that event, ChatResponseViewModel fires onDidChange, and ChatViewModel forwards it after invalidating _visibleItemsCache. Thus viewModel.getItems() in the autorun recomputes/filter-scans the transcript on each chunk. annotateSpecialMarkdownContent iterates and allocates a new representation of every response part. getPersistentWorkingProgress then filters pending confirmations and calls getPersistentProgressState/getPersistentActivityLabel, which perform several additional full-part scans. updateWorkingContent's equality check occurs only after all this work. This is synchronous renderer work on the streaming UI path and remains active when virtualization has removed the response row.
Findings.Recommendation: Track the latest response separately and derive a compact progress signature from only state that can change the sticky label (tail progress item, pending-confirmation candidates, active background counts, completion state). Coalesce content-change notifications to at most one update per animation frame, and skip annotation/progress recomputation when that signature is unchanged; preserve immediate updates for completion and blocking approval/question transitions.

Scenarios.Scenario: An active bottom-composer Chat or Agents-window response streams while the user reads the latest turn or scrolls earlier transcript rows out of virtualization.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: A provider response chunk is applied to ChatResponseModel, synchronously forwarded through ChatResponseViewModel and ChatViewModel, then the new sticky-progress autorun runs on the renderer's main-thread event stack before UI processing can continue. Existing transcript rendering also consumes the same model event; the sticky recomputation is additional work and is still performed when the response row is virtualized.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Effective cardinality is one latest response per widget, but each of E stream mutations scans T visible transcript items after cache invalidation and the P accumulated parts of that response multiple times. Long agent runs can accumulate many tool/progress parts, and token/progress chunking makes E large.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Updates are synchronous and serialized on the UI thread. There is no frame coalescing or limiter for the new autorun, so a burst of provider chunks produces a corresponding burst of recomputations.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: ChatViewModel's visible-items cache is invalidated before every forwarded response change, so the first getItems call in each autorun is cold and rebuilds the list; the second lookup in updateStickyProgress is warm only within that same run. Annotated response content and progress derivation are not cached, and unchanged labels are detected only after recomputation.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the synchronous event chain, cache invalidation, full annotation allocation, repeated part scans, and absence of coalescing are directly visible in the changed code and transitive implementations.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Provider chunk frequency, transcript length, and tool-part count vary, so exact frame-time impact is workload-dependent; long tool-heavy agent responses are a realistic high-cardinality trigger.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable medium-severity CPU/GC regression: the PR adds unthrottled collection-wide work to every streaming mutation, including when virtualization previously avoided response rendering.

Scenarios.Scenario: The active response completes, is canceled, or the widget switches to another chat session.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The response completion observable or view-model replacement synchronously clears/disposes the sticky part and its observation store. Session replacement also clears renderer pools through the existing updateViewModel path.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One sticky part and one observation store per widget/session; cost is constant per completion, cancellation, or session switch.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Lifecycle transitions are serialized on the UI thread; disposal cancels the autorun before the next session observation is installed.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cross-session cache is retained by the sticky component. Event-backed observables unsubscribe when the disposed autorun loses its last observer.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: MutableDisposable and DisposableStore ownership, DOM removal, and lazy event-observable unsubscription were traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Session-switch frequency varies but does not change the bounded ownership model.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding: cleanup is bounded and the old session/listeners are released.

Scenarios.Scenario: The chat input/composer is created and laid out with reference chips, narrow wrapping, theme changes, and scrolling.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: ChatWidget creates one empty sticky host in ChatInputPart, wires it to the list renderer, and CSS places a non-empty status before references. Layout and painting remain browser-local; the existing progress component is moved rather than duplicated.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Constant one host and at most one working-logo DOM subtree per eligible chat widget; status text length controls wrapping but not collection fan-out.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: DOM and CSS updates run on the UI thread. The existing working-logo animation uses visibility observation and its existing frame scheduling; the test-covered relocation keeps one logo rather than creating parallel animations.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache or remote data path is added. The logo's existing atlas/visibility behavior is unchanged and remains visibility-gated.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High after tracing ChatInputPart creation, ChatWidget wiring, CSS selectors, and ChatWorkingProgressContentPart/ChatWorkingLogo behavior.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Theme and narrow-layout reflows depend on host dimensions, but the diff adds no per-row or per-frame layout read/write loop.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable layout/rendering regression beyond the separately reported streaming recomputation; DOM cardinality is bounded and no forced-layout loop is introduced.

Scenarios.Scenario: Persistent progress is toggled, or the chat uses read-only, minimal, or input-on-top rendering.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Configuration or renderer-option changes synchronously recompute eligibility; disabled/read-only/minimal paths clear the sticky part and retain the existing transcript-owned progress behavior. Input-on-top/minimal hosts are not wired to a sticky container.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One eligibility check and at most one component create/dispose per setting/option transition per widget.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Transitions are synchronous and serialized; no asynchronous fan-out or queued work is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no persistent negative or positive cache. Configuration events are broad and also feed the reported autorun, but setting transitions themselves are infrequent and bounded.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High from changed option/configuration paths and fallback tests.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of simultaneously open chat widgets varies, but configuration changes are not a hot enough trigger to justify a separate finding.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding: fallback lifecycle and cardinality are bounded; broad configuration observation is subsumed by the streaming repeated-work finding.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass across all nine changed files. One introduced hot-path regression was submitted: sticky progress recomputes and reallocates over the transcript/latest response on every streamed model mutation without coalescing. Cleanup, DOM cardinality, animation visibility, CSS layout, fallbacks, and transitive expensive boundaries were checked; no subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network boundary is introduced by the diff.
